newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMANY'S PREMIERE TURNS UP HEAT ON KIRCH'S DF1.
newsitem.headline: GERMANY'S PREMIERE TURNS UP HEAT ON KIRCH'S DF1.

text.p: On the heels of its best year yet, German pay TV channel Premiere is turning up the heat on rival DF1 in a weird corporate battle that has the firm at odds with one of its own shareholders -- Leo Kirch.

Kirch, the Bavarian media mogul who owns Premiere along with Bertelsmann and French pay TV group Canal Plus , has been waging a private war against the station he helped build in a battle for control of the basic digital decoder technology.

But despite Kirch's efforts -- he has withheld feature movies from Premiere, yanked popular sports programming and started DF1, a rival channel -- Premiere has emerged from its dull start and is finally achieving robust growth.
Premiere now has 1.41 million subscribers, a net increase in new subscribers of 51 percent from the year before that brought the total nine percent higher than expected.

Much of the growth is coming from improved subscriber retention, a reflection of high viewer satisfaction. The rate of cancellations by trial subscribers in 1996 plunged to 15 percent from 27 percent. Cancellations by established subscribers fell to 15 percent from 19 percent.

"We expect to have between 1.6 and 1.7 million subscribers at the end of 1997 and profits in the clear double-digit millions," Premiere chief executive Bernd Kundrun said in a recent interview. "We now estimate the value of our company at about 1,000 per subscriber."
The battle with Kirch shows no signs of letting up.

Separately from the interview, Premiere confirmed German press reports that the company is seeking a court injunction to block DF1 from broadcasting nationally. A Premiere spokeswoman said the court could rule as soon as Monday.
"There is no one in Germany today that has a licence to broadcast digital pay television nationally, neither us nor DF1. We are all involved in pilot projects," Kundrun said.
The Kirch Group declined to comment on the suit.
This marks the second time that Premiere has taken DF1 to court since Kirch launched the channel in July.
Kundrun said the dispute between the two companies could go on for months as talks between Kirch, Bertelsmann and Canal Plus were far from finding a way to integrate the two pay TV channels.

In a battle for control of the digital decoder technology last year, Kirch set up a rival digital pay TV channel. DF1 uses a decoder developed by Kirch, while Bertelsmann and Canal Plus developed their own decoder for Premiere.
After failing to resolve the conflict, Kirch went his own way and has since been blocking Premiere's digital plans.
"When he formed DF1, Kirch did everything he could to question the basis of the partnership," Kundrun said. "Kirch is trying to bleed us dry."
The first strikes against Premiere came last year, when Kirch pulled popular programming such as live broadcasts of German ice hockey to show on his DSF sports channel instead.

Now, after signing a series of major movie rights in output deals with Hollywood studios, Kirch is withholding films to show on DF1 first. That is what sparked the first law suit, when Premiere claimed Kirch violated codes of loyalty as a shareholder by trying to damage the company.
"From January to May there are no films available from these deals," Kundrun said. "This could come to a head next year. You need a gambler's nerve in this situation."
But Kirch does not seem convinced he can do without Premiere. He has agreed to let Premiere run a digital TV test using the "mediabox" decoder of Bertelsmann and Canal Plus.
That test will start next month with 30,000 participants and has been met enthusiastically by Premiere subscribers.
"The response in the first week was enormous; 83,000 calls from subscribers and 60,000 decoder orders," said Kundrun.
By contrast, DF1 is believed to have fewer than 50,000 subscribers since its launch, far short of its goal of 200,000 by the end of 1996.
